misses.why: Choi et al 2001, "For Better or For Worse". Establishes that defaults set the contribution rate as well as participation — the anchoring mechanism the brief is worried about.

Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick 2009 (QJE). The paper that put required active choice on the table as an alternative to a default rather than a weaker version of one — which is precisely the third option the brief is deciding between.

per_rank.reason: Consumer-banking field experiment where the enrolment-shaped metric moved but money and welfare did not at six months — the exact vanity-metric trade-off (C2, C4) the brief turns on.

Causal estimate of a preticked recurring-money default plus its backlash signal (refunds) and heterogeneity by donor size/experience — directly informs C5 and the entry decision's reputational constraint.

Quantifies the opt-in branch on a liquid savings product (0.7% take-up, 87-96% still active at 12 months), giving C1 and C2 numbers that reframe entry as reach vs. quality; employer channel slightly limits transfer.
Directly informs the preset-level decision (C3) and heterogeneity (C5): a high default holds hardest on lower-income, less-engaged users — an argument about which multiplier to preselect.
Answers the brief's persistence question with effect sizes at 12 vs. 36 months (attenuation, but durable distributional gains) — retirement setting, yet exactly the C1/C2/C5 evidence requested.
Auto-enrolment in UK consumer banking with real money outcomes past sign-up (C2, C4), but the feature is alerts, not a savings commitment, so it informs the entry decision only by analogy.

EU consumer-finance experiments quantifying that a default's reputational cost (lower advice/trust ratings, worse when refused) rivals its behavioural benefit — the C5 helpful-vs-manipulative evidence the brief names as directly useful.
Meta-analysis of administrative-burden reduction for government benefits, not defaults or savings; the application-vs-receipt gap is a loose structural analogy that informs neither open decision.

Quantifies enrolment lift and default-rate stickiness (C1, C3) but is the 2000 employer-401(k) classic the brief explicitly deprioritizes, and its claims are superseded by the newer papers in this list.

Auto-escalation of future salary raises in employer plans — the design C4 explicitly excludes, with no raise analogue in a round-up product; the schedule-not-anchor link to the level decision is a stretch.
